title: Design a Hotel Booking System
summary: Search and book date-range inventory across thousands of properties — a range-overlap problem, unlike ticket booking's single-item lock.

slides.markdown:
The ask: a traveler searches "rooms in Austin, these three dates," books one, and the system never oversells that room for those dates.

This looks like [ticket booking](design-ticket-booking-system) at first glance — prevent double-selling scarce inventory — but the inventory here is a **date range**, not a single seat. Room 302 isn't simply available or not; it's available for *some* date ranges and booked for others, and a new request has to check for overlap against every existing booking, not against one boolean flag.

That range-overlap check, repeated across thousands of properties at search time, is the core of this design.

**Functional:** search availability by city and date range across many properties, hold a room during checkout, confirm a booking, cancel within policy.

**Non-functional:** search latency low enough to feel instant across a large city's worth of properties; an explicit overbooking policy — some hotels deliberately overbook by a small margin (like airlines), betting on cancellations, which is a business decision this design has to support, not just prevent.

The key framing: unlike ticket booking's zero-tolerance stance, hotel booking often *wants* a controlled amount of overbooking risk in exchange for higher occupancy — so "never oversell" isn't always the actual requirement here.

slides.sectionTitle: Back-of-envelope: properties, room-nights, and search vs booking QPS
slides.markdown:
A large city might list 5,000 properties averaging 100 rooms each — 500,000 rooms, and at 365 days of inventory, roughly 180 million room-night rows to reason about per city per year. Search traffic vastly outweighs booking traffic: for every completed booking, there might be hundreds of searches (browsing, comparing dates, checking prices).

That asymmetry matters: `searchAvailability` needs to be fast and can tolerate a few seconds of staleness, while the much rarer `confirmBooking` needs to be correct above all else. Optimizing search and booking as the same code path wastes effort on the 99% of traffic that doesn't need booking's strict guarantees.

Three calls:

- `searchAvailability(city, checkIn, checkOut, filters)` — the high-volume read path, served from a cache or search index that's refreshed frequently but need not be perfectly real-time.
- `holdRoom(propertyId, roomId, checkIn, checkOut)` — a time-boxed hold on a specific date range, the hot path where correctness matters most.
- `confirmBooking(holdId, paymentToken)` — finalizes the reservation once payment clears, same idempotency-key discipline as any payment-touching confirm call.

Notice the shape mirrors ticket booking's API almost exactly — search, hold, confirm — but every one of these now operates over a date range instead of a single discrete item.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: per-room-per-night rows vs a date-range calendar structure
slides.markdown:
| | Per-room-per-night rows | Date-range calendar structure |
|---|---|---|
| Shape | One row per (room, date) — simple, like ticket booking's per-seat row | A calendar/interval structure per room, storing booked ranges directly |
| Overlap check | A range query across many date rows | A native interval-overlap query against a small number of ranges |
| Storage | Large — 365+ rows per room per year, mostly "available" and unremarkable | Compact — only booked ranges are stored explicitly |
| Update cost | A single-night booking touches one row; a week-long stay touches seven | A booking is one interval insert, regardless of stay length |

**How to decide:** per-night rows are simpler to reason about and debug (this row said available, now it's booked), while a calendar/interval structure scales better as stay lengths grow — many real systems start with per-night rows for simplicity and only move to intervals once row volume becomes the bottleneck.

![Search fans out to a date-filtered search index across properties, rather than querying each property's live booking table](assets/search-fanout.svg)

Search doesn't query each property's live booking table directly — that would mean thousands of small queries per search. Instead it hits a search index that's refreshed on a short interval, trading a little staleness for speed across a large result set.

The live, authoritative check for double-booking still happens at `holdRoom` time against the real booking data — search is discovery, not the source of truth.

assets.alt: Search fans out to a date-filtered search index across properties, rather than querying each property's live booking table

slides.sectionTitle: Preventing overselling across overlapping date ranges
slides.markdown:
Two bookings for the same room conflict only if their date ranges **overlap** — booking June 10-12 and June 12-14 might or might not conflict depending on whether checkout and check-in on the same day counts as an overlap (usually it doesn't, since the room turns over). The overlap check has to be precise about these boundary conditions, not just a rough "do these ranges intersect."

`holdRoom` performs this as a single conditional operation: insert the new range only if no existing confirmed or held range for that room overlaps it, atomically, so two concurrent requests for overlapping ranges can't both succeed — the same atomic-write principle from ticket booking, applied to ranges instead of single rows.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: strict no-overbooking vs deliberate overbooking with a buffer
slides.markdown:
| | Strict no-overbooking | Deliberate overbooking with a cancellation buffer |
|---|---|---|
| Policy | Never book more rooms than physically exist | Allow a small percentage over capacity, betting on historical cancellation/no-show rates |
| Occupancy | Can leave rooms empty from last-minute cancellations | Higher average occupancy, closer to true demand |
| Risk | None of the "walk a guest" scenario | Occasionally has to relocate or compensate a guest when more show up than rooms exist |
| Who uses it | Smaller properties, or brands prioritizing guarantee over revenue | Large chains with reliable historical no-show data to model the buffer accurately |

**How to decide:** overbooking is a calculated bet, not a bug — it only works with good historical cancellation data for that specific property and season; a hotel with volatile or thin booking history should stay strict, since a bad bet means turning away a paying, present guest.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: booking flow — hold, payment, confirm, release-on-timeout
slides.markdown:
![Room booking flow: search, holdRoom, payment, confirmBooking, with expiry as the fallback](assets/room-booking-flow.svg)

The flow mirrors ticket booking's hold-then-confirm pattern closely: the hold is reversible by default (via expiry), and only `confirmBooking` succeeding makes the reservation permanent.

The difference is entirely in what's being reserved — a date range on a specific room, not a single discrete seat.

assets.alt: Room booking flow: search, holdRoom, payment, confirmBooking, with expiry as the fallback

slides.sectionTitle: The bottleneck: search fan-out across a large city
slides.markdown:
Booking-time contention is rarely the bottleneck here — unlike ticket booking's single-instant spike, hotel demand spreads across many properties and dates. The real bottleneck is **search latency**: a query for "Austin, these dates" has to check availability across thousands of properties and return ranked, filtered results in a couple hundred milliseconds.

The fix is the search index from earlier (§6) — pre-computing and caching availability summaries per property per date range so a search doesn't have to run a live overlap check against every property's raw booking data on every request. The trade is a small amount of staleness (a room shown as available that got booked moments ago) for search speed at scale — resolved definitively at `holdRoom` time.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: a single "rooms available" counter instead of per-date rows
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "I'll just track how many rooms are available per property — simpler than per-date-per-room tracking."

**Why it's wrong:** a single counter can't represent that a property has 10 rooms free next Tuesday but zero free next Friday — availability is inherently date-dependent, and collapsing it into one number either wrongly turns away a bookable guest or wrongly confirms a booking for a date that's actually full.

**Correct model:** track availability per room per date (or per date range), the same lesson as ticket booking's per-seat rows, applied along the date axis instead of the seat axis — the granularity has to match where the real contention lives.
